target_customer: Developers and companies that embed in-app chat, and later enterprises buying AI customer service agents
problem: Adding real-time messaging to a mobile app meant building and scaling chat infrastructure from scratch. Sendbird grew out of the team's own need for chat in a community app and sold it as a hosted API.
business_model: usage and subscription B2B API priced by user count and support level, later AI agent platform sold to enterprises
product_category: messaging API (chat as a service), later AI customer service agents

founders.name: John S. Kim
previous_startups: Paprika Lab (gaming studio, sold to GREE in 2012 per TechCrunch Feb 2016)
founders.background_notes: TechCrunch Feb 2016 says he was previously a pro gamer. Education not found in opened sources. Source: https://www.ycombinator.com/companies/sendbird and https://techcrunch.com/2016/02/12/sendbird-looks-to-help-developers-add-chat-functions-to-any-app

founders.name: Brandon Jeon
founders.background_notes: Listed as co-founder on the YC page; no further background found.

founders.name: Harry Kim
founders.background_notes: Listed as co-founder and CTO on the YC page; no further background found.

competitors.name: Layer
competitors.traction_then: won TechCrunch Disrupt 2013; Sendbird argued it lacked per-chat features such as unlimited participants in a room

competitors.name: Twilio
competitors.what: communications API company named as a possible entrant

technical_complexity.rationale: Reliable real-time chat at scale with per-room features is standard but demanding infrastructure; at launch it served 340 apps and about 2 million monthly users.

defensibility.rationale: Once an SDK is embedded in an app and history is stored, migrating is costly, but chat features are copyable and several rivals existed.

takeover_risk_then.outcome: TechCrunch named Twilio as a possible entrant in 2016. Sendbird remained independent and reached a $1.05 billion valuation in April 2021.

market_need_then: The team built chat for its own app Smile Mom and found no off-the-shelf option it liked; at launch Sendbird was live in 340 apps with about 2 million monthly users (TechCrunch, Feb 2016).

branding.name_origin: Company founder wrote that it was renamed from JIVER in early 2016 and combines send and bird, with bird added so the name would not sound too technical.

identity.logo: lowercase wordmark with an abstract bird to the left (USPTO description); the team's logo post says it explored bird shapes such as speech bubble and paper plane
identity.visual_style: purple palette with a bird mark

branding.brand_signature: the bird mark and purple color

rebrands.why: to expand more aggressively in the global market, per a company post

brand_strength.rationale: Clear, memorable name and consistent visual identity with documented design process, but no evidence of the brand itself driving growth; success was driven by developer product.

pivots.from: Smile Mom community app for nearby moms
pivots.to: Sendbird chat API as a product
pivots.why: the team built its own messaging and decided to productize it (YC launch post Feb 2016)

outcome_analysis: Sendbird turned an internal chat component into a developer API, reached 340 apps within weeks of the Winter 2016 batch, then raised a $16M Series A in 2017, $52M Series B in 2019 and a $100M Series C in 2021 at a reported $1.05 billion valuation. It stays independent and is pivoting to AI customer service agents. Layoff trackers show employee-reported cuts around 2023 and 2025, so growth has slowed from the 2021 peak.
notes: Company site about page returned 404. Recorded rounds total $168M against the company claim of $220M+, so earlier seed or later rounds are missing; the $220M figure is not itemized. Series B and C amounts and dates come from search result summaries of VentureBeat, Pulse 2 and AppDeveloperMagazine; Series C valuation from devops.com. Layoff evidence is from trackers (CB Insights 2023 list, TrueUp May 2025) and is unconfirmed.
